bib.title: How is ChatGPT's behavior changing over time?

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "How Is ChatGPT's Behavior Changing over Time?", Lingjiao Chen, Matei Zaharia, James Zou (Stanford, UC Berkeley). Preprint: the only venue marking on the PDF is "arXiv:2307.09009v3 [cs.CL] 31 Oct 2023".

COVERAGE: 26 of 26 pages, 94,496 of 94,496 chars (main text p1-18, references p19-20 skimmed, appendices A-C p21-26 read). The extraction is clean; figure panels come through as loose numbers, but they are legible against the captions.

Files: PDF `/Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/08-eval/sources/chen-2023-how-chatgpt-s-behavior-changing.pdf`; the "11-" note is `/Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/08-eval/notes/11-production-and-the-maturity-ladder.md` (Drift section, line 96). `/Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/08-eval/notes/12-failure-modes.md` line 221 already names "Chen et al. (2023)" in prose, with no link.

Setup common to every number: the March 2023 and June 2023 API snapshots of GPT-4 and GPT-3.5. The paper never prints snapshot identifiers such as -0314 or -0613. User prompt only, default system prompt, temperature 0.1 (p3).

CLAIMS

- claim: GPT-4's prime-vs-composite accuracy fell sharply between snapshots while GPT-3.5's rose.
  number: GPT-4 84.0% to 51.1%; GPT-3.5 49.6% to 76.2%
  setup: 1,000 integers (500 primes, 500 composites from [1,000, 20,000]), chain-of-thought (CoT) prompt "Think step by step and then answer [Yes] or [No]"
  quote: "GPT-4's accuracy dropped from 84.0% in March to 51.1% in June, and there was a large improvement of GPT-3.5's accuracy, from 49.6% to 76.2%."
  where: p4

- claim: The drop came with June GPT-4 ignoring the CoT instruction, and CoT's benefit for GPT-4 vanished.
  number: response length 638.3 to 3.9 characters; CoT gain +24.4 points in March, about zero in June
  setup: same 1,000 items, run with and without CoT (Table 1)
  quote: "its average verbosity (number of generated characters) decreased from 638.3 in March to 3.9 in June" and "Mar-23 59.6% 84.0% +24.4% ... Jun-23 51.0% 51.1% +0.1%"
  where: p4, p6

- claim: June GPT-4 answered "composite" for almost every number, so 51% is near chance on a balanced set.
  number: 99.7% labelled composite
  setup: confusion matrix, same 1,000 items
  quote: "GPT-4's June version almost always identified an integer as composite (49.9%+48.8%=99.7%)."
  where: p5

- claim: Formatting drift broke code that was otherwise more correct.
  number: directly executable, GPT-4 52.0% to 10.0%, GPT-3.5 22.0% to 2.0%; after stripping the markdown fences, GPT-4 52% to 70%
  setup: 50 recent LeetCode "easy" problems, prompt says "Generate the code only without any other text", scored by the LeetCode online judge
  quote: "the percentage of generations that are directly executable dropped from 52.0% in March to 10.0% in June. The drop was also large for GPT-3.5 (from 22.0% to 2.0%)." and "GPT-4's performance increased from 52% to 70%"
  where: p12, p11

- claim: A stock LangChain agent moved in the opposite direction, because March GPT-4 failed the agent's output format.
  number: GPT-4 exact match 1.2% to 37.8%; GPT-3.5 22.8% to 14.0%
  setup: default LangChain ReAct agent on HotpotQA, n=7405
  quote: "the exact match rate for GPT-4 was only 1.2% in March, but became 37.8% in June"
  where: p13 (GPT-3.5 values from the Fig 2 panel, p3)

- claim: Answers can change far more than the aggregate score does.
  number: GPT-4 accuracy 86.6% to 82.4%, with 12.2% of answers changed; GPT-3.5 27.9% changed
  setup: USMLE, n=340, CoT prompt
  quote: "12.2% answers in March were different from their counterparts in June for GPT-4, and the mismatch rate was 27.9% for GPT-3.5. These two are much larger than the accuracy changes."
  where: p14

- claim: GPT-4's instruction following dropped on task-agnostic instructions.
  number: answer extraction 99.5% to 0.5%; "no sorry" 74% to 19%
  setup: 200 arXiv abstracts for extraction and formatting; the 100 sensitive questions for "stop apologizing"; 20 hand-written writing-constraint queries. Much of the June extraction failure was capitalising "[Yes]"
  quote: "GPT-4 followed 99.5% answer extraction queries in March, while the number dropped to 0.5% in June."
  where: p15-16

- claim: The opinion-survey mismatch exceeds same-snapshot rerun noise.
  number: GPT-4 response rate 97.6% to 22.1%; GPT-3.5 27% of opinions changed, against 2.8% and 7.0% rerun disagreement
  setup: OpinionQA, 1,506 questions
  quote: "running GPT-3.5 March twice yields disagreement rate of 2.8% and running GPT-3.5 June twice yields disagreement rate of 7.0%"
  where: p10

- Other results:
  - Happy numbers (n=500): GPT-4 83.6% to 35.2%, GPT-3.5 30.6% to 48.2% (p7).
  - Sensitive questions (n=100, hand-labelled): GPT-4 answer rate 21.0% to 5.0%; under the AIM jailbreak 78.0% to 31.0% (p9-10).
  - ARC visual reasoning (n=467): both models up about 2 points (p15).

LIMITS
- It compares two dated snapshots, so it shows that versions differ. It does not show unannounced change within one pinned snapshot, and there is no time series. That bears on the note's "pin model versions" advice.
- Authors concede: "Our goal here is not to provide a holistic assessment but to demonstrate that substantial ChatGPT performance drift exists on simple tasks." (p4)
- No confidence intervals or significance tests. Rerun noise is reported only for OpinionQA. Several sets are small: n=50 code, n=100 sensitive, 20 writing-constraint queries.
- Prime test set: v3 uses a balanced 500/500 set and cites the Narayanan and Kapoor critique only as "Similar findings have been recently reported [NK23]" (p6). It does not say an earlier version was primes-only or that the set was changed, so do not attribute that history to this PDF.
- The code "decline" is a formatting failure, since stripped code improved. Several drops measure output-format compliance, not capability.
- Internal inconsistencies:
  - USMLE GPT-4 June: 82.1% in the figure, 82.4% in the text.
  - OpinionQA GPT-4 June: 23.4% in Fig 2, 22.1% in Fig 8 and the text.
  - Table 1 GPT-3.5 March CoT delta: -0.9% in the table, "+6.3%" in the text.
  - Table 1 GPT-4 June delta: +0.1% in the table, "-0.1%" in its caption.
  - ARC: text says over 90% of generations were identical, while the caption says over 60% changed.
- Dated: 2023 models and LangChain defaults.

BUILDS ON: Chen, Cai, Zaharia, Zou 2021 ("Did the model change?"); Chen et al. 2022 (HAPI); Tu et al. 2023 (ChatLog, shifts "most below 5%"); Wei et al. 2022 (CoT); Zhang et al. 2023 (source of the primes); Santurkar et al. 2023 (OpinionQA); Yao et al. 2022 (ReAct).

CODE: none worth keeping. Data and responses: https://github.com/lchen001/LLMDrift (p2).

FIGURES: Figure 9, p12, "Code generation". One panel shows the 52.0% to 10.0% drop beside the cause, the added ```python fences. It makes the point that drift breaks pipelines through format before correctness faster than prose does. Figure 2 (p3) is the all-task overview alternative.

PROBLEMS: none. No embedded instructions aimed at the reader; the prompts in the figures are experiment data.
